title: Burj Khalifa, Dubai
body:
Burj Khalifa, Dubai rises 828 metres over Dubai and was completed in 2010 to a design by Adrian Smith of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. It is the tallest completed building in the world, with a triple-lobed footprint derived from a desert flower, and it holds offices, residences, and an observation deck.

Burj Khalifa is the public fact against which every later supertall tower is measured, and its construction record — concrete pumped to record heights, a spire assembled at altitude — is a standard case study in tall-building engineering.

title: Empire State Building, New York
body:
Empire State Building, New York rises 381 metres to its roof, 443 metres with its antenna, over Manhattan, and was completed in 1931 to a design by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon. It held the title of world's tallest building for nearly forty years, and its Art Deco crown remains one of the most recognised silhouettes on earth.

The Empire State Building is a public landmark of the steel-frame age, completed in just over a year during the Great Depression, and it still draws millions of visitors to its observatories each year.

title: Shanghai Tower, Shanghai
body:
Shanghai Tower, Shanghai rises 632 metres over Shanghai and was completed in 2015 to a design by Gensler. Its twisting form turns 120 degrees from base to top, reducing wind load, and its double skin encloses sky gardens at intervals up the tower.

Shanghai Tower is the tallest building in China and a leading example of sustainable supertall design, with wind turbines at its crown and a facade system that cuts energy use well below comparable towers.

title: One World Trade Center, New York
body:
One World Trade Center, New York rises 541 metres, a symbolic 1,776 feet, over Lower Manhattan, and was completed in 2014 to a design by David Childs of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. It stands on the site of the original World Trade Center as a commercial tower and a memorial anchor for the rebuilt district.

One World Trade Center is a public fact of post-2001 New York: a tower whose height, security design, and memorial setting are all part of its civic meaning.

title: Taipei 101, Taipei
body:
Taipei 101, Taipei rises 508 metres over Taipei and was completed in 2004 to a design by C. Y. Lee & Partners. Its segmented bamboo-like form and its giant tuned mass damper, visible to visitors, made it a landmark of structural engineering in a typhoon and earthquake region.

Taipei 101 held the world's-tallest title from 2004 to 2010, and its damper ball remains a public demonstration of how engineers tame wind and seismic sway.

title: Petronas Towers, Kuala Lumpur
body:
Petronas Towers, Kuala Lumpur rise 452 metres over Kuala Lumpur as a twin pair, completed in 1998 to a design by Cesar Pelli. Linked by a skybridge at the 41st and 42nd floors, they were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004 and remain the world's tallest twin towers.

The Petronas Towers are a public symbol of Malaysia's modernisation, their Islamic geometric patterns giving a national identity to a supertall form.

title: Willis Tower, Chicago
body:
Willis Tower, Chicago rises 442 metres over Chicago and was completed in 1973 to a design by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, with structure by Fazlur Rahman Khan. Its bundled-tube frame of nine tubes, stepping back at three heights, made it the world's tallest building for twenty-five years.

Willis Tower, formerly the Sears Tower, is the classic bundled-tube case study, and its glass-floored Skydeck ledges are a public attraction on the 103rd floor.

title: Chrysler Building, New York
body:
Chrysler Building, New York rises 319 metres over Manhattan and was completed in 1930 to a design by William Van Alen. Its terraced crown of stainless-steel arches, sunburst windows, and eagle gargoyles made it the world's tallest building for eleven months, until the Empire State Building surpassed it.

The Chrysler Building is a public Art Deco masterpiece, and its crown — built in secret inside the tower and raised in one dramatic lift — is one of the great stories of New York construction.
